network.overall_strategy: On chemical merit, the network is built around the only intermediate-resolved prebiotic route to the proline skeleton: Patel-style surface cyanosulfidic chemistry. Hydrothermal glutamate/ornithine ideas and discharge or ice detections are not expanded into productive branches because the supplied literature treats their proline-forming steps as speculative or detection-only. Ten distinct pathways are realized as combinatorial variants at four experimentally motivated branch points within the Patel backbone: sulfide-only vs Cu-accelerated nitrile reduction, sulfide-only vs Cu-accelerated photodeoxygenation, sulfide-only vs Cu-accelerated late desulfurative HCN capture, and two aminonitrile hydrolysis regimes. All chemical branches first yield racemic proline; a separate final phase-behavior node resolves or amplifies that pool toward L-proline, because no abiotic route is known to make L-proline directly. Free cyanohydrin and inferred 1-pyrroline are treated as mechanistic transients inside atom-balanced nodes so sulfur redox stays explicit and hydrolysis remains separated from chiral amplification.

reactions.name: Cu(I)-catalyzed HCN-acetylene coupling to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic post-impact or evaporitic surface pool; acetylene plausibly supplied by carbide hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Cu(I)-mediated cyanovinylation of acetylene by HCN.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. identify Cu(I)-catalyzed cross-coupling of HCN and acetylene as the entry to the proline and arginine branch, giving acrylonitrile (Patel et al., 2015). This is the best-supported prebiotic start to the proline skeleton, although its geochemical plausibility depends on local Cu availability and on acetylene release from impact-derived carbides; those constraints are emphasized by Ranjan et al. (2018).

reactions.name: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: NH3-rich local pulse in anoxic water.

reactions.mechanism: Conjugate aza-Michael addition across the activated alkene.
reactions.reasoning: Ammonia addition to acrylonitrile to give beta-aminopropionitrile is explicitly discussed as a proline precursor in the cyanosulfidic network (Patel et al., 2015). The aza-Michael addition is chemically straightforward in water and does not require a separate catalyst.

reactions.name: UV/H2S reduction of beta-aminopropionitrile to beta-aminopropionaldehyde

conditions.other: UV irradiation in sulfide-bearing, mildly alkaline water; laboratory analogs used 254 nm-equivalent light.

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox reduction of the nitrile to an imidoyl or iminium level followed by hydrolytic release of the aldehyde, with sulfide oxidized to elemental sulfur.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. use UV/H2S photoredox to reduce nitriles to aldehydes within the cyanosulfidic network (Patel et al., 2015). This node writes that chemistry as the atom-balanced net beta-aminopropionitrile + H2O + H2S -> 3-aminopropanal + NH3 + S; the detailed radical sequence is abbreviated, but sulfur redox is explicit. Surface sulfide availability remains a known environmental limitation (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Cu-photoredox UV/H2S reduction of beta-aminopropionitrile to beta-aminopropionaldehyde

conditions.other: UV irradiation in sulfide-bearing water with locally available Cu; laboratory analogs used 254 nm-equivalent light.

reactions.mechanism: The same photoredox nitrile-to-aldehyde conversion as rxn_003, accelerated by Cu(I)/Cu(II) cycling.
reactions.reasoning: Same chemical destination as rxn_003, but with Cu(I)/Cu(II) photoredox acceleration, which Patel et al. report can speed UV/H2S reductions without changing the overall transformation (Patel et al., 2015). This variant is useful where local Cu is available, but it inherits the same Cu-abundance and staged-delivery critiques discussed by Ranjan et al. (2018).

reactions.name: HCN capture and cyclothioamidation to the cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide

conditions.other: Transient cyanohydrin formation and intramolecular ring closure occur in the same HCN and H2S pulse.

reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde capture by HCN to a cyanohydrin, sulfur insertion or thioamidation of the nitrile, then intramolecular cyclization to the observed cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. report aldehyde capture by HCN followed by sulfur chemistry to alpha-hydroxythioamides, including a cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide on the proline branch (Patel et al., 2015). For compactness, the free cyanohydrin is treated here as a mechanistic transient inside the atom-balanced node rather than as a separate graph node.

reactions.name: UV/H2S photodeoxygenation of the cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide to gamma-butyrothiolactam

conditions.other: UV irradiation with sulfide acting as stoichiometric reductant in anoxic surface water.

reactions.mechanism: Photodeoxygenation of the alpha-hydroxythioamide to the cyclic thiolactam with explicit sulfur oxidation.
reactions.reasoning: Photodeoxygenation of the cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide gives gamma-butyrothiolactam as the only deoxygenated thioamide observed on this branch (Patel et al., 2015). The balanced net uses H2S as reductant and writes elemental sulfur plus water explicitly rather than hiding the redox chemistry in abstract H2 bookkeeping.

reactions.name: Cu-photoredox UV/H2S photodeoxygenation of the cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide to gamma-butyrothiolactam

conditions.other: UV irradiation in sulfide-bearing water with local Cu available for photoredox cycling.

reactions.mechanism: The same photodeoxygenation as rxn_006, accelerated by Cu(I)/Cu(II) photoredox.
reactions.reasoning: Cu(I)/Cu(II) photoredox can accelerate the same UV/H2S photodeoxygenation chemistry (Patel et al., 2015). This alternative keeps the same stoichiometric outputs as rxn_006 but represents a more Cu-rich local surface microenvironment.

reactions.name: Photodesulfurization and HCN capture of gamma-butyrothiolactam

conditions.other: Intermittent HCN delivery traps an inferred 1-pyrroline in sulfide-bearing solution under UV irradiation.

reactions.mechanism: Photodesulfurization of the thiolactam to an inferred 1-pyrroline followed by Strecker-type HCN capture to the cyclic alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. convert gamma-butyrothiolactam to pyrrolidine-2-carbonitrile, the proline alpha-aminonitrile, in 32% over the final two steps; the intervening cyclic imine is inferred rather than isolated (Patel et al., 2015). This node therefore encodes the atom-balanced net photodesulfurization plus HCN capture. Ritson (2021) notes that the cyclic proline aminonitrile is unusually resistant to retro-Strecker reversion, strengthening this branch relative to acyclic amino nitriles.

reactions.name: Cu-photoredox photodesulfurization and HCN capture of gamma-butyrothiolactam

conditions.other: Intermittent HCN delivery traps the inferred cyclic imine in sulfide-bearing solution with local Cu photoredox acceleration.

reactions.mechanism: The same imine-forming photodesulfurization and HCN capture as rxn_008, accelerated by Cu(I)/Cu(II) cycling.
reactions.reasoning: Same net chemistry as rxn_008, but with Cu-photoredox acceleration in sulfide-bearing solution, consistent with Patel et al.'s general observation that Cu(I)/Cu(II) cycling speeds cyanosulfidic reductions (Patel et al., 2015). The imine-trapping logic is the same; only the local catalytic regime differs.

reactions.name: Aqueous hydrolysis of proline aminonitrile to DL-proline

conditions.other: Long residence time in standing water or geothermal pools; racemic product expected.

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydration via the amide to the carboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of pyrrolidine-2-carbonitrile to proline is chemically standard and is the necessary completion of the Patel branch, but Patel et al. did not report a proline yield from the aminonitrile (Patel et al., 2015). This node is therefore plausible yet unquantified for proline specifically. Ritson (2021) supports accumulation of the proline aminonitrile because, unlike many acyclic aminonitriles, it resists reversion to the cyanohydrin.

reactions.name: Wet-dry mineral-assisted hydrolysis of proline aminonitrile to DL-proline

conditions.other: Evaporation-rehydration on clay and phosphate-rich shores; racemic product expected.

reactions.mechanism: Heterogeneous hydration and hydrolysis of the aminonitrile under wet-dry concentration cycles.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative alternative to rxn_010: wet-dry concentration on clay or phosphate-rich shores could accelerate the same aminonitrile-to-amino-acid hydrolysis by increasing local concentration and residence time. No proline-specific prebiotic yield is reported in the provided literature, so this node is explicitly marked speculative and is included only as a chemically plausible surface completion step (Patel et al., 2015; Ritson, 2021).

reactions.name: Eutectic phase amplification and resolution of DL-proline

conditions.other: Freeze-thaw or evaporation-crystallization in concentrated brine; requires a tiny prior L-ee and is represented schematically as 2 DL-proline -> L-proline + D-proline.

reactions.mechanism: Solution-solid partitioning of a racemic compound or eutectic, enriching the mobile phase in one enantiomer and the complementary phase in the other.
reactions.reasoning: No abiotic route in the provided literature makes L-proline directly. Proline is nevertheless unusually favorable for physical ee amplification: its solution composition is constrained by eutectic phase behavior, with 54-58% ee measured in MeOH and EtOH and far stronger but non-prebiotic CHCl3 cosolvate behavior (Klussmann et al., 2006). This node abstracts conservative prebiotic freeze-thaw or evaporation partitioning of a slightly L-biased DL pool into L-proline and a complementary D-rich phase; it is a resolution or amplification step, not an asymmetric synthesis. A prior tiny L bias is required and could in principle come from CPL or other symmetry-breaking processes, but it is not generated here (Modica et al., 2014).

pathways.name: Baseline downstream sulfide-only branch with aqueous hydrolysis
pathways.description: Cu is used only in the entry coupling; all downstream photoredox steps are sulfide-only, the aminonitrile hydrolyzes in standing water, and the resulting DL-proline is phase-resolved.

pathways.name: Baseline downstream sulfide-only branch with mineral hydrolysis
pathways.description: The same downstream sulfide-only photoredox sequence as P1, but aminonitrile hydrolysis is assigned to wet-dry mineral surfaces before chiral resolution.

pathways.name: Late Cu-assisted capture branch
pathways.description: Early downstream steps remain sulfide-only, but the final thiolactam to aminonitrile conversion uses Cu-assisted photoredox before aqueous hydrolysis and resolution.

pathways.name: Cu-assisted deoxygenation only
pathways.description: Aldehyde release is sulfide-only, photodeoxygenation to the thiolactam is Cu-accelerated, and the late aminonitrile formation and hydrolysis follow the aqueous variant.

pathways.name: Cu-assisted deoxygenation and late capture with mineral hydrolysis
pathways.description: Sulfide-only aldehyde release is followed by Cu-accelerated thiolactam formation and Cu-accelerated late HCN capture, then wet-dry mineral hydrolysis and resolution.

pathways.name: Cu-assisted aldehyde release only
pathways.description: Cu acceleration is introduced only at the beta-aminopropionitrile-to-aldehyde step; later photodeoxygenation and thiolactam capture are sulfide-only, followed by aqueous hydrolysis and resolution.

pathways.name: Cu-assisted aldehyde release plus late capture
pathways.description: Cu accelerates aldehyde release and the final thiolactam-to-aminonitrile conversion, while photodeoxygenation remains sulfide-only and hydrolysis occurs on wet-dry mineral surfaces.

pathways.name: Cu-assisted aldehyde release and deoxygenation
pathways.description: Cu accelerates the nitrile-to-aldehyde and alpha-hydroxythioamide-to-thiolactam steps, while the late HCN capture is sulfide-only; aminonitrile hydrolysis then occurs in bulk water before resolution.

pathways.name: Fully Cu-assisted downstream photoredox with aqueous hydrolysis
pathways.description: All three downstream photoredox-sensitive stages use Cu acceleration before standing-water hydrolysis and eutectic resolution.

pathways.name: Fully Cu-assisted downstream photoredox with mineral hydrolysis
pathways.description: All three downstream photoredox-sensitive stages use Cu acceleration, but the aminonitrile is completed to DL-proline by wet-dry mineral hydrolysis before final phase resolution.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Best-aligned branch with Patel-style sulfide-only downstream chemistry and simple aqueous hydrolysis. The backbone to proline aminonitrile is chemically credible and literature-supported. Main weaknesses are rxn_008, which under-specifies the late Patel photoredox step because sulfide/HS- and explicit UV conditions are omitted, rxn_010, which needs 2 H2O for atom balance and has no reported prebiotic yield for proline formation, and rxn_012, which is a phase-resolution bookkeeping step rather than a demonstrated L-selective synthesis.
suggestions: Add explicit HS-/H2S and UV conditions to rxn_008 or justify a reagent-free desulfurization.
Write rxn_010 as mol_012 + 2 mol_005 -> mol_013 + mol_003 and state hydrolysis conditions and yield uncertainty.
Replace rxn_012 with an explicit crystallization or eutectic amplification model that includes a seed ee and physically justified environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This keeps the strong Patel backbone, but the mineral-assisted hydrolysis step is less well anchored because no specific mineral or direct proline aminonitrile hydrolysis evidence is given. rxn_011 also needs 2 H2O for balance. The final L-resolution node remains the dominant weakness.
suggestions: Name the mineral phase and wet-dry regime for rxn_011 and cite evidence for aminonitrile hydrolysis on that substrate.
Balance rxn_011 with 2 H2O.
Model L-enrichment as phase behavior or separation rather than a stoichiometric conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Using Cu-assisted late capture is literature-compatible as an acceleration variant, but rxn_009 still omits the sulfide or photoredox context expected from Patel-type desulfurization. Cu availability is plausible only in localized settings. Hydrolysis to proline remains unquantified and L-selection is not mechanistically resolved.
suggestions: Specify Cu source or loading, UV regime, and whether HS-/H2S participates in rxn_009.
Balance rxn_010 with 2 H2O and note that yield to proline is not reported.
Provide a prebiotic seed-asymmetry source or demote rxn_012 to a non-stoichiometric amplification or separation node.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cu-assisted deoxygenation is a reasonable Patel-style acceleration and keeps the rest of the route close to the best-supported backbone. The same late-step issue remains: rxn_008 under-specifies the photodesulfurization and HCN-capture chemistry, and the L-proline step is still a separation or amplification proxy rather than a demonstrated synthesis.
suggestions: Keep rxn_007 but specify Cu photoredox conditions and likely mineral context.
Add HS-/H2S and UV detail to rxn_008 if that is the intended chemistry.
Revise rxn_012 to an environmentally grounded eutectic or crystallization process with explicit seed ee.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This branch combines two condition-heavy extensions beyond the directly supported core: Cu-assisted late capture and an unspecified mineral hydrolysis. That does not make it impossible, but it is less well evidenced than the aqueous-hydrolysis variants. The resolution step to L-proline remains inadequately grounded.
suggestions: State the mineral used in rxn_011 and why it is present in the surface setting.
Clarify whether rxn_009 requires HS-/H2S as stoichiometric reductant or only Cu photoredox.
Represent enantiomeric enrichment with phase partitioning rather than net molecular creation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cu-assisted nitrile reduction is literature-compatible and may improve the difficult aldehyde-release step. Otherwise this is the same strong Patel backbone. However, the network still relies on an under-specified late capture step, an unquantified aminonitrile hydrolysis, and a weakly modeled L-resolution node.
suggestions: Define Cu mineral source and UV conditions for rxn_004.
Balance rxn_010 with 2 H2O and optionally include prolinamide as an intermediate.
Replace the 'Biochemical' label on rxn_012 with a physically justified eutectic or crystallization environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This variant is chemically coherent and follows Patel-style logic, but it compounds Cu assumptions at the aldehyde-release and late-capture stages. rxn_009 still lacks explicit sulfide or photoredox specification, and the endgame from DL-proline to L-proline remains only partially literature-supported.
suggestions: Provide explicit conditions for rxn_004 and rxn_009, including Cu source and UV wavelength.
Balance rxn_010 with 2 H2O and note uncertainty in prebiotic hydrolysis rate and yield.
Add a seed-ee source and realistic solvent or phase conditions for any L-enrichment step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cu assistance at nitrile reduction and photodeoxygenation is defensible and close to the experimentally accelerated Patel chemistry. As in the other aqueous branches, the weakest points are the late thiolactam-to-aminonitrile step as written and the final chiral-resolution node.
suggestions: Spell out the UV, Cu, and HS- conditions for rxn_004 and rxn_007.
Amend rxn_008 to reflect the intended photoredox reductant if sulfide is required.
Model L-proline enrichment as a crystallization or amplification process rather than a stoichiometric reaction.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is closest to the fully accelerated downstream Patel-style laboratory logic, so the core racemic skeleton-forming chemistry is fairly strong. Environmental realism is weaker because multiple Cu-dependent steps require localized copper-rich settings, and rxn_009 still omits the reductant or photoredox details expected for the final capture. The hydrolysis and L-resolution steps remain the main evidence gaps.
suggestions: Justify Cu availability across all photoredox steps.
Balance rxn_010 with 2 H2O and give a realistic hydrolysis environment.
Downgrade rxn_012 to an ee-amplification or separation event with explicit solvent and seed asymmetry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The fully Cu-assisted plus mineral-hydrolysis branch is the most condition-heavy variant. It remains chemically imaginable, but it is the least well constrained environmentally and evidentially. The proline hydrolysis step is still unquantified, and the final L-proline node is not a true stoichiometric synthesis.
suggestions: Specify mineral identity and local Cu source for the surface setting.
Balance rxn_011 with 2 H2O and cite support for mineral-assisted hydrolysis of proline aminonitrile.
Use a non-stoichiometric resolution or amplification node for chirality.

evaluation.network_feedback: Connected and mostly well specified network with strong literature alignment to the Patel/Sutherland cyanosulfidic route, the only intermediate-resolved prebiotic path to the proline skeleton; it also sensibly avoids treating detection-only or metabolism-first ideas as demonstrated production routes. The RDKit check finds no unbalanceable reactions, but rxn_010 and rxn_011 need 2 H2O, and rxn_012 is only balanceable as bookkeeping for resolving a racemic pool; mol_013 should be treated as a state node, not a distinct molecular species in a synthetic step. Chemistry is strongest through proline aminonitrile and reasonably plausible, though unquantified, to DL-proline. The main weaknesses are that rxn_008 and rxn_009 under-specify the late Patel photoredox desulfurization and HCN-capture by omitting explicit HS-/H2S conditions, the surface environment lacks explicit pH, UV, and staged-delivery detail, and the final L-proline node requires an external seed ee plus a realistic eutectic or crystallization environment rather than the current 'Biochemical' label. Overall this is a good Patel-derived racemic proline network, but not yet a high-confidence abiotic L-proline network. Not approved.
